idiom_name: defer f.Close() + an idempotent Close() error method (io.Closer)
implementation_notes: Go replaces the Dispose protocol with the defer statement: acquire, immediately defer the release, and deferred calls run in LIFO order after the surrounding function returns - including while a panic unwinds - so no exit path can skip them, which is why the go.dev article presents defer as the cleanup idiom. The release itself is an ordinary method (Close() error, conventionally io.Closer); ownership and cascade stay the implementer's job - a type that owns sub-resources closes them in its Close, and since the language has no disposed-state machinery you make Close idempotent with sync.Once or a nil check. runtime.SetFinalizer exists only as an unpredictable backstop for leaked handles and must never be the mechanism you rely on. The classic structure survives only inside the Close implementation itself.
pitfalls: defer is function-scoped, not block-scoped: a defer inside a loop holds every handle open until the function returns - wrap the loop body in a closure to bound the lifetime.
`defer s.Close()` discards the returned error; when the release error matters (flush, fsync), defer a closure that merges it into a named error result.
Go gives no compile-time ownership: two functions may both defer Close() on a shared pointer, which is safe only because Close is idempotent - without sync.Once it double-releases.
